    Lesson 1 · 30 minutes

    Context and memory: what your assistant can actually see

    By the end of this lesson you can decide, for each piece of information in your makerspace assistant, whether it goes in the context, gets saved between sessions, or gets looked up when needed, and say why.

    Objective O3: context and memory in an agentAbout 30 minutesOne-page cheat sheet
    Why this matters for you

    Your assistant has to answer from long machine manuals and remember each student's training status between visits. It also has a small model budget. All three come down to one design question: what text does the model receive on each call? Your design review will go better if you can answer that with numbers.

    In this lesson
    1. Warm-up
    2. The context window
    3. Between steps
    4. What size costs you
    5. Between sessions
    6. Retrieval: finding the right page
    7. Notes and compaction
    8. Worked example and practice
    9. Summary
    10. Go further

    Warm-up 2 min

    Answer from memory before you open each answer. The effort of recalling is what helps it stick.

    Recall 1

    From what two sources can a language model know anything when it writes a reply?

    Check your answer

    What it learned in training, and the text it is given. Today is all about the second source, because that is the one your program controls.

    Recall 2

    Name the repeating cycle that makes up an agent, including how it ends.

    Check your answer

    The model gets a goal and tools, asks for an action, the action is carried out, and the result goes back to the model. This repeats until the model gives a final answer or a limit is reached. Today you look closely at what "goes back to the model" really involves.

    The context window 4 min

    Start with an example. You hire a very capable helper for your makerspace desk. They have one odd limit: they remember nothing about your desk from one moment to the next. Every time you want something, you hand them a folder. They read it, write one reply, and forget it.

    If the laser cutter's rules are not in the folder, the helper has only their general knowledge. They might guess, and the guess might sound confident.

    That folder is like the model's context. Context is the set of tokens the model is given when it produces output ({a(A,"Anthropic Engineering")}). A token is a small unit of text that the model processes, often a piece of a word. Different models split text differently, so the same page can have different token counts ({a(G,"Claude glossary")}).

    The context window is the limited amount of room for those tokens. In the Claude documentation, which makes a concrete reference here, it includes the system prompt, all the messages (including tool results, images and documents) and the tool definitions. The reply being written counts too ({a(C,"context window docs")}). The system prompt is the standing instructions your program supplies, such as "You help students at the makerspace."

    So for your assistant, one call's window might hold:

    • your instructions to the assistant;
    • descriptions of tools such as the calendar check and manual search;
    • the student's question and any earlier messages;
    • results that tools have returned;
    • the new output the model is writing.

    The window has a hard size, which depends on the model. In the Claude API, for instance, a request whose input alone is too long is rejected with an error, and a reply can be cut off if it fills the remaining room ({a(C,"docs")}). Other services may handle overflow differently, so check yours.

    Fitting is not the same as working well

    Picture a workbench. A bigger bench holds more parts, but burying the one screw you need under 500 others does not help you find it. Models have a related problem. As the token count grows, accuracy and recall can degrade. This is called context rot ({a(C,"docs")}). It is a gradual slope, not a sudden cliff, and Anthropic's engineers advise treating context as a limited resource. Their goal is the smallest set of useful, high-signal tokens that gets the job done ({a(A,"article")}).

    {mix("“With a big enough window, we can stop worrying”",'

    This is tempting because a large window removes the error you would hit first. But it does not make extra text free or harmless. You still send and pay for the tokens, and unrelated text can make the useful part harder to use. A window size tells you what fits. It does not tell you what you should send.

    Between steps: the program carries everything 4 min

    A student asks, "Can I use the laser cutter Friday?" Your agent needs several model calls to answer. Call 1 asks for a calendar check. How does call 2 know what the question was?

    Your program tells it again. It keeps a list: the question, the model's tool request, and the tool's result. For call 2, it sends the instructions, tool definitions and that list. For call 3, it sends the longer list.

    The general idea is that a model call does not carry your conversation over to the next call. The Claude documentation puts it this way for its Messages API: it is stateless, meaning you always send the full conversation history ({a(M,"Messages API guide")}). Some services offer to store the history for you; the same guide describes such a feature in beta. That changes who holds the list. It is still saved history being supplied to the model, not the model learning your conversation.

    {f1}

    This kept history is often called short-term memory: the record of the ongoing conversation within one session. LangChain's documentation uses the term for history tied to one conversation thread ({a(L,"LangChain memory overview")}). A session here means one visit or conversation. A step is one turn around the agent loop.

    As turns pile up, earlier messages stay in the history and the window fills ({a(C,"docs")}). That happens by default only because the history keeps being included. Your program can choose to shorten or remove old material. LangChain notes that long histories may not fit, and that many applications benefit from removing or forgetting stale information ({a(L,"overview")}).

    Worked trace

    Here is what your program holds at each point:

    MomentSent to the modelAdded afterward
    Call 1Instructions, tools, questionRequest: check calendar; then its result
    Call 2All aboveRequest: search manual; then its result
    Call 3All aboveFinal answer to the student

It does not restore other text unless that text is in it."), ("The model must work without that exact question",True,"It may infer something from the calendar result, but it was never given the question in this call.")], "It must work without the question. It might guess the goal from other text, which makes this bug easy to miss.")}

    What size costs you 4 min

    Model use is commonly billed by the token. Claude's pricing page, for example, prices input tokens and output tokens separately ({a(P,"pricing")}). Since each call sends its own input, text that you resend is counted again on each call.

    Worked example: one question, three calls

    These sizes are made up but handy for arithmetic. Instructions are 600 tokens, tool definitions 900, and the question 50. Each tool request is 40 tokens. The calendar result is 150, the manual search result is 2,000, and the final answer is 200.

    1. Call 1 input: 600 + 900 + 50 = 1,550.
    2. Call 2 input: everything in call 1, plus the first request and calendar result: 1,550 + 40 + 150 = 1,740.
    3. Call 3 input: everything in call 2, plus the second request and manual result: 1,740 + 40 + 2,000 = 3,780.
    4. Total input: 1,550 + 1,740 + 3,780 = 7,070. Total output: 40 + 40 + 200 = 280.

    Notice the difference between two numbers. The largest window use is call 3: 3,780 input plus 200 output, or 3,980. The billed input is the sum over calls, 7,070. One tells you whether it fits; the other drives cost.

    {f2}

    Now suppose you paste a 60,000-token manual into the instructions instead. For a fair rough comparison, keep every other number the same, including the search step. Each of the three calls grows by 60,000. Total input becomes 7,070 + 180,000 = 187,070 tokens, over 26 times as much.

    At an invented price of 1 dollar per million input tokens, 1,000 such questions cost about 7 dollars in input with the smaller design and 187 dollars with the pasted manual. Output costs extra. Check real prices for your model.

    Services may offer prompt caching, which reuses repeated input so it costs less. It can change the comparison a lot. In Claude's documentation, cached tokens still count toward the context window ({a(C,"docs")}). So calculate cost with your provider's real rules, and remember that a discount does not make the window roomier.

    Calculate

    A different request takes two calls. Call 1 has 1,200 input tokens. The model's tool request is 30 tokens, and the result is 500. Call 2 sends all of it. What is the total input across both calls?

    Show the solution

    Call 2 input is 1,200 + 30 + 500 = 1,730. Total input is 1,200 + 1,730 = 2,930. If you got 1,730, you found the biggest call but left out what you sent the first time.

    Between sessions: only what you save and load 4 min

    On Monday, Sam tells the assistant, "I prefer short answers." Sam returns on Thursday in a new conversation. Will the assistant know?

    Only if your system saved that fact on Monday and put it into context on Thursday. Long-term memory is information stored so it can be used across sessions ({a(L,"LangChain")}). It might be a database row, a file or a collection of notes. It lives outside the context window.

    Think of a paper logbook at the desk. Writing in it keeps the information. It helps only when someone opens the right page and reads it.

    {f3}

    So every memory feature needs answers to four questions:

    1. Write: what is worth saving, and who or what saves it?
    2. Store: where is it, and which student does it belong to?
    3. Read: when does the program load it, or let the model request it?
    4. Update: what happens when it becomes wrong?

    Writing can happen while the agent handles the request. That makes the memory available right away but adds delay. It can also happen later in a background job, which may leave other conversations without the new information for a while ({a(L,"LangChain")}).

    LangChain also borrows three labels: semantic memory for facts, episodic memory for past experiences or actions, and procedural memory for instructions on how to act ({a(L,"overview")}). You do not need three databases. The labels just help you ask what kind of thing you are saving.

    Training status: a record, not a recollection

    Here is a design recommendation for your team. Treat the makerspace's official training record as the one source of truth. Have your program or a tool such as check_training_record look up the current status when needed. Do not rely on an old chat note saying "Sam is trained." Training can be added, expire or be revoked, and a copy may not change with it. If your makerspace has no such record yet, your team needs a reliable one that only authorized staff can update. A student's claim in chat should not grant access.

    Also have the program fix whose records get loaded, using the signed-in student's identity. One student's notes should never appear in another's context.

    {mix("“It's an assistant, so it remembers past visits”",'

    Chat products can make memory feel built in. When you build your own system, do not assume it. If Thursday’s call includes neither Monday’s conversation nor a saved note, and no tool fetches them, Monday is unavailable. A product that does remember has some part that saves information and supplies it later.

    Retrieval: finding the right page 5 min

    A student asks, "What material can I not cut on the laser cutter?" A good human helper does not reread every manual. They find the laser cutter's materials section and read that.

    Retrieval means finding relevant stored information and bringing it into context. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) combines that search with the model's writing: documents from an outside source are passed into the context window ({a(G,"glossary")}). Retrieval does not retrain the model. The page is simply more input.

    A common setup works like this ({a(R,"Anthropic on retrieval")}):

    1. Split the documents into chunks, small passages often no more than a few hundred tokens.
    2. Build an index you can search.
    3. For a question, find the most relevant chunks.
    4. Add those chunks to the model's input.
    {f4}

    There are two useful ways to search. Keyword search matches words or phrases. It helps with exact things such as an error code; one common ranking method is called BM25. Semantic search aims to match meaning. It uses embeddings, lists of numbers that represent a text's meaning. It can connect "what is unsafe to cut" with a passage headed "Prohibited materials," but may miss an exact code. Systems can combine both ({a(R,"source")}).

    For a first prototype in Python, you might begin with simple keyword search over chunks, test it on real student questions, and add semantic search if it misses differently worded ones. That is a starting suggestion, not a rule.

    Where retrieval fails

    Imagine a chunk that says only, "Never leave it running unattended." Which machine is "it"? Splitting a document can strip away the context that gave a passage its meaning. Anthropic's fix, called contextual retrieval, adds a short explanation to each chunk before indexing it ({a(R,"source")}). A simple step in the same spirit is to keep the machine name, manual title, section and page with each chunk.

    The search can also return the wrong chunk or miss the right one. The model then writes from poor input. When you test, print the retrieved chunks first. If the right rule is not there, fix the search before you rewrite the prompt. Ask the assistant to cite the manual page, and to say when the retrieved text does not answer the question. Citations help people check, though they do not guarantee correctness.

    Up front or on demand?

    Your program could search before the first model call and include the results. Or you could give the model a search_manuals tool so it searches only when needed. The second is called just-in-time retrieval: the agent holds lightweight pointers or search tools and loads data while it works. It can save space, but exploring takes longer than using data fetched in advance, and a badly guided agent can chase dead ends. A hybrid loads a little up front and fetches the rest later ({a(A,"article")}).

    Retrieval is not required for every document set. Anthropic's retrieval article says a knowledge base under 200,000 tokens, about 500 pages, can be placed whole in the prompt, with prompt caching to cut cost ({a(R,"source")}). That is advice from one provider at one time. Your window, accuracy tests and per-question budget decide what suits you.

    Notes and compaction 3 min

    Suppose a student spends 40 messages troubleshooting a failed print. You do not want to resend every long tool result forever. But you cannot throw away "we already replaced the nozzle."

    Structured note-taking means the agent regularly writes notes to storage outside the context window and brings them back later ({a(A,"article")}). Anthropic gives a to-do list and a notes file as examples. For your student, a note could be:

    Goal: fix poor first layer on printer 2
Tried: cleaned bed; replaced nozzle
Result: problem remains
Next: check bed leveling (manual p. 14)

    This note is invented for illustration. It can support the next step, and if saved under the right student and job, a later session.

    Compaction means summarizing a long context and continuing in a fresh one that starts from the summary ({a(A,"article")}). A lighter approach clears old tool results that are no longer needed. The risk is that a summary drops a detail that later matters. Keep important facts, decisions and open problems. Test your summaries on long conversations.

    ToolWhat it doesMain risk
    RetrievalFinds relevant stored textWrong or missing passage
    NotesSave progress or facts outside the windowWrong or out-of-date note
    CompactionReplaces long history with a summaryLost detail

    These can work together. A saved note can itself be retrieved. The common thread is that your system chooses what text reaches the next call.

    {check("A repair chat is nearly too long. Which compacted summary best prepares the next call to continue the job?",[ ("Student had a printer problem; we discussed several fixes",False,"This loses which fixes were tried and what happened, so the agent may repeat them."), ("Printer 2: new nozzle failed; check leveling next",True,"It keeps the machine, a tried fix, its outcome and the next action."), ("Student was friendly, patient and eager to get printing",False,"Tone may be pleasant to know, but it gives nothing needed to continue the repair.")], "The printer 2 summary keeps the facts that affect the next action. A real one should also keep other fixes tried, such as cleaning the bed.")}

    Worked example and practice 3 min

    Worked example: place each piece of information

    Ask three questions: Is it needed in this call? Must it outlast the session? Can it change or is it too big to send every time?

    1. Safety instructions for the assistant's behavior: short and always needed, so include them in each call. Real access rules, such as who may book, should also be enforced in program code.
    2. Machine manuals: long, and only parts matter per question. Store and index them; retrieve labeled chunks.
    3. Calendar: changes often. Check it live with a tool. A result from last week is not current availability, and even an earlier result today can go stale, so recheck when booking.
    4. Answer-length preference: lasts across visits and is small. Save it per student, load it at the start, and let the student change it.
    Your turn: the follow-up

    Return to the three-call laser cutter example. In the same session, the student sends a 30-token follow-up: "What did that safety rule mean?" The model can answer in one call.

    (a) If your program keeps the whole history, including the 200-token final answer, how big is the new input? (b) Suppose it replaces the 2,000-token manual result with a 100-token note holding the key rule and page number. How big is it now? (c) Name one risk of doing that. (d) The student returns next week. What would need to happen for the assistant to use that note?

    First step: begin with call 3's input of 3,780.

    Show a solution

    (a) 3,780 + 200 + 30 = 4,010 tokens.

    (b) 4,010 − 2,000 + 100 = 2,110 tokens, assuming nothing else changes. This does not count any cost of creating the note.

    (c) The note may omit an exception or distort the rule. For a safety question, keep the page reference and fetch the original wording again when needed.

    (d) The note must have been saved outside the session under the right student, then loaded or fetched into the new context. For safety rules, check that the manual has not changed.

    Summary 1 min

    • The context window is limited room for what one call reads and writes. Fitting does not guarantee good use.
    • Between steps, your program (or a history service) keeps the conversation and supplies it again. Resent input adds up across calls.
    • Between sessions, information must be saved, then loaded or fetched.
    • Retrieval selects stored text; notes record facts and progress; compaction shortens history. Each can fail.
    • For changing facts such as bookings and training, check the official record.

    Say it in your own words: without looking, explain to a teammate how your assistant could use something a student said last week. Name every step from then to now. Type your explanation in the chat if you would like me to check it.

    Go further

    Read next: {a(A,"Effective context engineering for AI agents")}. It is the best single next step because it connects context limits, just-in-time retrieval, notes and compaction from an agent builder's view. It is written by a model provider, so treat its advice as expert guidance to test. You can skip the sub-agent part for now.

Your 30-minute lesson on context and memory is ready: `lessons/0001-context-and-memory.html`. By the end, you should be able to decide what your assistant sends with every call, what it saves between sessions and what it looks up when needed.

It covers:
- the context window, and why text that fits can still cause problems
- what carries over between agent steps, with a short Python-style trace
- a three-call token and cost example, using made-up sizes and prices
- saving information between sessions
- finding the right part of a manual, and how that search can fail
- notes and summarizing long chats
- practice questions with feedback, plus a follow-up exercise where some steps are left for you

**For your design review:** I recommend that the assistant check each student's training status in an official record when it needs it, rather than rely on a saved chat note. A copied note can become out of date. This is my design advice, so check which training records your makerspace actually has.

I also made a one-page cheat sheet, `cheatsheets/context-and-memory.html`, and updated `RESOURCES.md` and `NOTES.md`. Quiz 0002 is ready when you are, ideally after a short break. Your two attempts at quiz 0001 are still ungraded, and I can grade them if you like.
